title: The elephant in the dark
hookLine: people touch an elephant in a dark room and call it a fan, a pillar, a throne (Rumi, Masnavi 3.1259ff)
tomorrow: Abba Moses and the leaking basket

lines: A DARK ROOM, A LARGE VISITOR.
cards: Think of a family argument about something that happened years ago. Your sister remembers one thing, your dad another, and you remember a third, and you'd swear to it. Everyone was there.
Everyone is sure. And somehow nobody's lying: each of you touched a different part of the same afternoon.
The Persian poet Rumi, writing in the twelve hundreds, told a story about exactly this, set in a dark room, with a very large visitor inside.

teach.h: AN ELEPHANT IN A DARK HOUSE.
teach.b: It's in his long poem, the Masnavi, in its third book. Travelers bring an elephant to a town where no one has ever seen one, and keep it in a dark house.
People crowd in, but it's too dark to see, so each one reaches out and touches.

teach.h: A PIPE, A FAN, A PILLAR, A THRONE.
teach.b: One hand finds the trunk: this creature is like a water pipe. Another finds the ear: no, it's like a fan. Another wraps her arms around a leg: it's a pillar.
Another pats the back: it's shaped like a throne. Each description is honest, each is about something real, and each is wrong about the whole. Then comes the line the story turns on.
If each of them had held a candle, Rumi says, the difference would have gone out of their words. Nobody needed to shout louder. They needed light.

teach.h: ASK WHAT THEIR HAND IS TOUCHING.
teach.b: Rumi was a Muslim scholar and Sufi teacher, and he uses the story to say something about the limits of our senses: the hand can only know what it touches.
Readers have taken it in many directions since, and people disagree about how far to push it.
An older cousin of the story appears in the Buddhist Udana, where a king has blind men describe an elephant, and they end up in a fistfight.
So the picture has traveled. When someone describes something completely differently from you, maybe one of you is simply wrong. Or maybe you've got the ear, and they've got the leg.
Before arguing, ask what their hand is touching.

how: Readers of Rumi's Masnavi often tell the elephant in the dark when talking about the limits of what any one person perceives, and teachers in many settings use it to open conversations across disagreement.

o: a Sufi dance of turning in slow circles
a dark house where an elephant was kept
Rumi's long poem of stories and teachings

each described something real. each was wrong only about the whole.

games.q: you're in the dark house. you've touched the elephant's ear, and it's plainly a fan. your neighbor insists it's a pillar. what does Rumi say would settle it?
o: whoever touched it first is right
a vote of everyone in the room
games.why: a candle. with light, he says, the difference would have gone out of their words. each hand was honest; none could see the whole.

practice: Bring to mind a person who sees some small, real matter differently from you, and picture the two of you in the dark room, each with a hand on the elephant. Ask yourself gently: what part might they be touching that I'm not?
Then picture asking them one honest question that begins, how do you see it?

wordCard.voice: Masnavi. Rumi's long poem, where hands in a dark room each touch an elephant, each honest, each partial, until a candle could have ended the argument.

orig.note: Persian: elephant. Rumi wrote the Masnavi in Persian, and the story's heading speaks of an elephant in a dark house.

carryVoice: Your line: bring a candle. Every hand in the dark is honest, and only partly right. Day seventy-two, done.
